items.correct: No — enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.
items.misconception: Yes, enzymes are tiny living organisms.
items.random_wrong: Enzymes are a type of sugar.
items.why: Enzymes are made of protein and speed up reactions, but they are not living things.

items.q: What happens to an enzyme after it catalyses a reaction?
items.correct: Nothing — it is unchanged and can be reused many times.
items.misconception: It is used up and must be replaced each time.
items.why: Catalysts, including enzymes, are not consumed; one molecule works on substrate after substrate.

items.q: What does heating an enzyme to a high temperature do?
items.correct: It denatures the enzyme, changing the active site so it stops working.
items.misconception: It makes the enzyme work faster and faster with no limit.
items.random_wrong: It turns the enzyme into a substrate.
items.why: Above the optimum, heat changes the enzyme's shape (denaturing); the substrate no longer fits the active site.

items.q: Can one type of enzyme speed up any reaction?
items.correct: No — enzymes are specific to their substrate (lock and key).
items.misconception: Yes, a single enzyme works on any molecule.
items.random_wrong: Only if the reaction happens in the stomach.
items.why: Each enzyme's active site is complementary to one substrate, so enzymes are highly specific.
